title: Lochana Dasa Thakura
html:
The Singer of the “Chaitanya-mangala”

Lochana Dasa Thakura is the Vaishnava poet who composed the “Sri Chaitanya-mangala,” a Bengali poem on the life and pastimes of Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, and a disciple of Narahari Sarakara Thakura of Shrikhanda, an intimate associate of the Lord. He never saw the Lord Himself: he was born when Mahaprabhu was already residing in Nilachala, and he composed his poem after the Lord's disappearance — one of those who treasured the memory of His pastimes. In the poem and in his songs he signs himself “Lochana Dasa”; later Vaishnava poets call him “Thakura Lochana,” and the “Prema-vilasa” calls him Lochana or Lochana Dasa. The “Chaitanya-charitamrita” does not speak of him; nor is he found in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika,” and the sources are silent on who he is in Krishna's eternal pastimes.1 All we know of his life comes from his own words, from a few lines in later Vaishnava books, and from tradition.

Kogram: Family and Childhood

Lochana Dasa appeared in 1523 (1445 of the Shaka era) in the village of Kogram, or Ko-gram, in the Rarh country. The village lies in the Katwa subdivision (mahakuma) of Bardhaman district, about ten miles — five kroshas — north of Guskara station, near Jhamatpur; Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati gives the place the same way: “in Kogram, in the Katwa subdivision of Burdwan district.” One of the biographies adds that the Thakura's house stood not far from the river Ajay.2 By our calendar (Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math) his appearance day is Gaura-pratipad, the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Narayana (≈ Pausha); in 2027 it falls on 8 January. One of the biographies, citing “some,” gives the same day.

His family were vaidyas, physicians of Rarh (radhiya-vaidyas): so say Lochana himself, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, the “Prema-vilasa” and the biographies.3 His father was Sri Kamalakara Dasa, his mother Srimati Sadanandi. At the end of the “Chaitanya-mangala” Lochana himself tells of his family:4

“Having completed the account in four parts, I have made it known. I was born in the vaidya caste and live in Kogram. My pious mother is named Sadanandi: born from her womb, I long for Krishna. My father who gave me birth is Kamalakara Dasa: by his grace I tell the tale of Gora's [Gaura's] glories.” (“Chaitanya-mangala,” Shesha-khanda, 94+59–61)

He goes on to recall his mother's family. Her people and his father's lived in one village; his grandmother was named Abhaya Dasi, and his maternal grandfather was Sri Purushottama Gupta, “purified by many tirthas and content in austerity.” “In my mother's family and my father's I am the only son,” Lochana writes. The only son was especially loved: wherever he went he was petted, and no one could teach the spoiled boy. It was his grandfather who taught him his letters — “by beating and strictness”; and Lochana gratefully bows at his feet: “by his grace I write the life of Chaitanya” (ibid., 94+62–67). The biographies also say that he studied in his grandfather's house, and according to one of them he spent most of his childhood with his grandparents.

From his very childhood his heart was given to Gauranga, and he remained indifferent to worldly things; according to one of the biographies, while still a boy he was blessed with the company of Sri Gauranga's devotees. He was married very young, as was the custom of the time. His father-in-law's house was in the village of Kakut near Amedpur.

A Renounced Householder

Lochana became a householder, but the world held no attraction for him: he spent his time with Gaura's devotees, in talks about Krishna.

There is a wondrous tradition about his detachment. His wife had been given to him as a child, and she lived with her parents. The girl was growing up and the time was approaching for her to move to her husband's house, but her parents saw that their son-in-law was wholly detached from the world, and they grew anxious. They went to his guru, Narahari Sarakara, and Narahari told his disciple to go to his father-in-law's house. Lochana had not been there for a long time and could not find the house; he asked the way of a young woman he met in the village street and addressed her, as is the custom in Bengal, as “ma,” “mother.” When he reached the house, he realized that he had asked the way of his own wife. From then on, it is said, he saw his wife no longer as a spouse but as a mother, and to the end of his days, renounced from the world, he served Sri Guru and Gauranga.

There is no neglect of duty or coldness toward his wife in this story. It speaks of the vairagya of Narahari's disciple: his heart was so full of Gaura that he saw a mother in every woman, and a word spoken out of custom became for him a truth for life.

At Narahari's Feet

Lochana's guru was Narahari Sarakara Thakura of Shrikhanda, one of Gaura's best-known associates. In the bloom of youth Lochana came to Shrikhanda, found his gurudeva and sought refuge at his feet. Narahari came to love him and gave him initiation (diksha); the biographies call Lochana Narahari's “dear” disciple, devoted to him alone. Lochana gladly settled with his guru in Shrikhanda — the “Prema-vilasa” says just this: “he is a disciple of Sri Narahari and lives in Shrikhanda.” Narahari trained him in kirtana, and later told him to write the life of the Lord. Lochana took this order to heart, and so the “Sri Chaitanya-mangala” came to be, a holy narrative full of the nectar of Gauranga's pastimes. In many places of the poem, as Srila Bhaktisiddhanta observed, Lochana calls himself a follower of Narahari.

Love for the guru fills the whole book. At its very beginning Lochana writes:

“Thakura Sri Narahari, master of his servant's life — my hope is in his feet; low though I am, I long to sing the virtues of Gaura — this is what Lochana Dasa trusts in.” (“Chaitanya-mangala,” Sutra-khanda 9)

“Without him I have no friend in the three worlds; I praise Narahari Dasa, ocean of Gaura's virtues,” he says further on (ibid., 33); and, asking the Vaishnavas' blessing, he turns to his guru once more: “My Thakura, Prabhu Narahari Dasa — I bow and humbly pray: fulfil my desire” (ibid., 61). So too the poem ends. In his closing word Lochana calls Narahari Dasa “the Thakura of my life” and “the giver of prema-bhakti to me”: all he was able to tell is by his guru's grace (Shesha-khanda, 94+42, 94+68–69).

At the end of the Sutra-khanda Lochana glorifies his guru as an eternal associate:

“In Vrindavana he was named Madhumati, a dear companion of Radha, a treasury of sweetness. Now, in the Kali age, Narahari, companion of Gaura, is the keeper of the treasury of the prema of Radha and Krishna.” (“Chaitanya-mangala,” Sutra-khanda 645–646)

As Narahari's disciple, Lochana says that Gadadhara Pandita and Narahari are Mahaprabhu's dearest associates: “Glory to the Lord of the life of Narahari and Gadadhara!” (Sutra-khanda 12). More than once he paints Gaurasundara with Gadadhara at His left, Narahari at His right and Raghunandana at His feet. He glorifies his guru's nephew, Raghunandana Thakura, as well — both in the opening of the poem (Sutra-khanda 36) and at the end of the Sutra-khanda (647–651), where he recalls how the boy Raghunandana fed the Deity a sweet ball.

After the Guru's Departure

Narahari Sarakara left this world on the Krishna-ekadashi of the month of Agrahayana, and in memory of his departure a great festival was held in Shrikhanda. Lochana served the Vaishnavas there. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” tells how he and Yadunandana Thakura adorned the honoured guests, Krishna Mishra and Gopala, the two sons of Sri Advaita (9.410, 9.592):

“Sri Yadunandana and Sri Lochana — the two of them — took flower garlands and fragrant sandal.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 9.591)

One of the biographies adds that he distributed these garlands and sandal to all who had gathered (for the day of the festival see “Bhakti-ratnakara” 9.513). Thus Lochana's name was preserved by Narahari Chakravarti, the author of the “Bhakti-ratnakara”; one of the biographies takes care to note that this Narahari — a native of Renga in Murshidabad district, known also as Ghanashyama Dasa — is not the Narahari of Shrikhanda who was Lochana's guru.

The “Prema-vilasa,” a late book and not reliable in everything, speaks of the same days. After the departure of Gadadhara Dasa and Narahari, Raghunandana, “taking Lochana with him,” came to Katwa (Katoa) to Yadunandana Chakravarti, a disciple of Gadadhara Dasa, and together they fixed the day of the memorial festival; and some days before the festival Raghunandana came to Katwa again “together with Lochana and others” (19.126, 136).5 To the great festival at Kheturi Raghunandana came from Khanda, “bringing with him Lochana Dasa and other devotees” (19.322).

Narahari Chakravarti remembers Lochana in the “Namamrita-samudra” as well, where he addresses a prayer to each of the Lord's associates:

“Thakura Lochana, grant me always this one thing: may my mind drown in Gauranga's pastimes!” (“Namamrita-samudra” 69)

The “Sri Chaitanya-mangala”

Lochana's principal work is the “Sri Chaitanya-mangala.” Its basis is Murari Gupta's Sanskrit poem about the Lord, known as Murari's “Kadacha” and called by Srila Bhaktisiddhanta the “Sri Chaitanya-charita.” Lochana himself tells how that book came about and how he took up his own:

“All that the Lord did from His birth in childhood, how from beginning to end He spread prema — about all this Damodara Pandita questioned him, and he told him everything from beginning to end in due order. So came about a book of Gauranga's deeds composed in verse — the dialogue with Damodara, issued from Murari's mouth. Hearing it, I was filled with love, and I tell of Gaura's deeds in a sung narrative, a panchali.” (“Chaitanya-mangala,” Sutra-khanda 53–56)

He says the same again in his conclusion: Murari Gupta, a vaidya and intimate of the Lord, composed in shlokas a poem on Gaura's glories to deliver the people, and it became the basis for all; hearing it, Lochana, greedy for its sweetness, forgot his own faults and composed the account in panchali form (Shesha-khanda, 94+44–48).6 Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes that Lochana began the book from the childhood pastimes of Gaurasundara recorded by Murari Gupta and took them as his source-evidence. Following Murari's “Kadacha,” Vrindavana Dasa, Lochana and others described the Lord's pastimes; from Murari Lochana took, for example, the account of the Lord's meeting with Ramananda Raya.

In form the “Chaitanya-mangala” is a panchali, a sung narrative of the kind long composed and sung in Bengal: according to one of the biographies, Lochana followed the pattern of East Bengali panchalis — the “Lakshmir panchali,” the “Shanir panchali,” the “Manasa-bhasan” and others. Such poems were composed in song-metres of five kinds; so too Srila Bhaktisiddhanta defines the book: “a book of the panchali kind, that is, a work composed in song-metres of five kinds.” One of the biographies observes that poets in Bengal had long composed sacred songs in various metres, and that the panchali kind especially served the glorification of the Lord.

The very title speaks of the book's aim. Mangala means “blessing”: to hear of Mahaprabhu's pastimes is the highest blessing for all living beings. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains: by the pastimes of Sri Chaitanyadeva the bonds will fall from the living beings bewildered by maya and blessing will come — therefore the narrative of Him is called the “Sri Chaitanya-mangala”; He Himself is full of the highest blessing.

The language of the poem was valued not by Vaishnavas alone. Ashutosh Dev, in his “New Bengali Dictionary,” calls Lochana a pioneer of Bengali literature in the “language of facts,” that is, the narration of actual events, and of verse in the matravritta metre; according to one of the biographies, Lochana was the first to compose Bengali verse in metres based on the counting of morae (matra) and was one of the first historical writers of Bengal.

When the poem was written is not known for certain.7 By tradition, Lochana wrote it seated on a stone beneath a flowering tree. It is said that the manuscript in his own hand is kept in the village of Kandra (Kadra) near Guskara station, with Sri Pranakrishna Chakravarti.

The poem is divided into four parts (khandas) — the Sutra-, Adi-, Madhya- and Shesha-khanda; Lochana himself names them in his conclusion (Shesha-khanda, 94+50–52). In Srila Bhaktisiddhanta's edition, according to his survey of the parts, there are two sections in the Sutra-khanda, seven chapters in the Adi-khanda, sixteen in the Madhya-khanda and three in the Shesha-khanda.8 The poem opens with blessings and obeisances to the guru and the Vaishnavas. Then, following the dialogue of Narada and Uddhava from the “Jaimini-bharata,” Lochana explains why Krishna descended as Gaura, tells of Rukmini, of Parvati and mahaprasada, and then of the Lord's birth and childhood and all His pastimes, up to His mercy to the poor brahmana from Dravida and the six-armed form shown to King Prataparudra.

What the “Chaitanya-mangala” means for Vaishnavas and how it should be read was best said by Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, who published the poem in 1922. Many, he writes, hesitate to accept its historical statements: part of its information was gathered “on the basis of dreams,” and full regard for the truth of pure bhakti is not seen everywhere; yet no one can doubt the reliability of its geographical indications, its clear description of Sri Chaitanya's ideal of renunciation gladdens the reader, and Lochana's love for Gaura draws the love of Gaura's devotees. Therefore, where the “Chaitanya-mangala” differs from the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” and the “Chaitanya-bhagavata,” we follow them.9

Much that Vrindavana Dasa only touched on, Lochana describes in detail. The Vaishnavas of old already noticed this; the “Anuraga-valli” says:

“What remained in it [the “Chaitanya-bhagavata”] in the form of sutras Thakura Lochana told in particular: the book Sri Chaitanya-mangala, full of rasa, he revealed in the form of songs — that was his intent.” (“Anuraga-valli” 1.6–7)

Such, for example, is the account of the Lord's last night in Navadvipa before His sannyasa and of His conversation with Vishnupriya, which is not found in Vrindavana Dasa. The Lord speaks to her of the illusory nature of worldly ties and shows her His four-armed form: through this conversation He instructs all living beings. This is no worldly family drama. The words about maya on the Lord's lips refer to the jiva's ties in this world, not to Him Himself nor to His eternal consort; and Vishnupriya, as one of the biographies explains, nourishes the joy of the independent Gaura, and in her separation from Him true devotees see the pastime of Vrajendranandana in the mood of Radha, not a shadow of possessive feeling. Those who distort this account, taking it for worldly love, are prakrita-sahajiyas.

Lochana sings of Vishnupriya more than once. At the beginning of the poem he glorifies her:

“I praise Vishnupriya-ma, [the lady] of Navadvipa: her ornament is the rosy feet of the Lord.” (“Chaitanya-mangala,” Sutra-khanda 22)

Following Murari, he also gives the words of her father, Sanatana Mishra. And when the Lord has left home, Lochana describes her weeping:

“At Vishnupriya's weeping the earth splits; beasts, birds, creepers, trees — even the stones weep.” (“Chaitanya-mangala,” Madhya-khanda 14.15)

Vishnupriya is the Lord's eternal consort, His potency (Bhu-shakti), and her separation from the Lord is no worldly grief.

The songs of the “Chaitanya-mangala” are sung to this day in various places of Rarh, as jhumur or the songs of the “Ramayana” are sung — so wrote Srila Bhaktisiddhanta. They were sung in the house of Narottama Dasa Thakura too; the “Prema-vilasa” says of Lochana:

“Sri Lochana Dasa is born of a vaidya family; he is a disciple of Sri Narahari and lives in Shrikhanda. The songs of the Chaitanya-mangala composed by him are always sung in Narottama's house. First the Sri Chaitanya-mangala is sung, and after that the Krishna-mangala is sung.” (“Prema-vilasa” 19.413–415)

Two “Chaitanya-mangalas”

Vrindavana Dasa's book, too, was at first called the “Sri Chaitanya-mangala,” and later became known as the “Sri Chaitanya-bhagavata.” To this name, it is thought, Lochana alludes when at the beginning of his poem he glorifies its author:

“With one mind I praise Sri Vrindavana Dasa, by whose song, the Bhagavata, the world is enchanted.” (“Chaitanya-mangala,” Sutra-khanda 35)

Who gave Vrindavana's book its new name, and why, is told in different ways. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes in the introduction to his “Gaudiya-bhashya”: Lochana Dasa Thakura, a disciple of Narahari Sarakara, wrote a book with the same title, and to distinguish the two books Vrindavana Dasa later named his own the “Sri Chaitanya-bhagavata” — at the request of his mother, Narayani Devi. In his preface to the “Chaitanya-mangala” he also relates a tradition: Lochana's book was written somewhat before Vrindavana's, and when Vrindavana's mother said so, his book had to be renamed.10 According to one of the biographies, Vrindavana's book was renamed when Lochana gave his poem the same title; according to others, “some think” the name “Chaitanya-bhagavata” was given to it by Lochana Dasa and Krishnadasa Kaviraja, and most likely by Kaviraja, for he compares Vrindavana Dasa to Vyasa:

“Veda-vyasa told the pastimes of Krishna in the Bhagavata; the Vyasa of Chaitanya's pastimes is Vrindavana dasa.” (CC, Adi 8.34)

Be that as it may, there was no rivalry between the two books. One of the biographies observes that among Gaura's associates there is no enmity born of envy — otherwise Narahari's disciple Lochana would not have glorified the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” and its author, though Vrindavana Dasa does not mention his guru. The same book notes that the name of Jiva Gosvami appears neither in Murari's “Kadacha,” nor in the “Chaitanya-bhagavata,” nor in Lochana's “Chaitanya-mangala.”

Songs

Besides the “Chaitanya-mangala,” Lochana is credited with the “Prarthana,” the “Durlabha-sara,” a collection of songs, the “Padavali” or “Dhamali,” a Bengali verse rendering of Ramananda Raya's “Jagannatha-vallabha-nataka” (its Sanskrit verses rendered into Bengali songs bearing Lochana Dasa's signature), and a verse rendering of the “Rasa-panchadhyayi.”

Above all the devotees honour his songs about Nityananda. It is said that Lochana grew anxious: in the “Chaitanya-mangala” he had glorified his guru as the dearest to Mahaprabhu but said little of Nityananda's glory — had he not thereby offended Nityananda's feet? And to make amends he composed several songs on Nityananda's greatness. This anxiety is the humility of a Vaishnava, to whom even a shadow of inattention to Nityananda seems a fault — not an acknowledged offence.

Three such songs are known: “Nitai guna-mani amara, nitai guna-mani…” (“Nitai is my jewel of virtues”), “Akrodha paramananda nityananda raya…” (“Nityananda Raya, free of anger, the highest bliss”) and “Parama karuna pahun dui jana, nitai gaurachandra…” (“Supreme mercy are the two Lords, Nitai and Gaurachandra”). In the first, Nitai brings a flood of prema to Gauda and drowns everyone in it, passing over neither the fallen nor the sinful, and at every threshold gives away the love that even Brahma cannot attain; whoever has not honoured Nitai has ruined himself. In the second, Nitai, free of anger and pride, wanders through the town, gives the great mantra of the holy name at the doors of the fallen and, with a straw between His teeth, begs: “Buy Me — worship Gaurahari.” In the third, Nitai and Gaurachandra are the crown of all avataras, the source of nothing but bliss: at the telling of Them beasts and birds weep and stones melt, while Lochana laments that he himself is sunk in worldliness and Yama punishes him with the fruits of his karma.

The song “Parama karuna” was especially dear to Srila A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada. Explaining it, he said that Nitai and Gaura are the very quintessence of all avataras, and the path They give is joyful — to sing and dance; there is only one condition — to give up sense enjoyment and sing “Hari, Hari” with firm faith. If the Lord inspired even the animals of the Jharikhanda forest to chant the holy name, how much more can people be drawn to the chanting.

Many other padas about Gaura circulate in the anthologies — the “Padakalpataru” and the “Gaura-pada-tarangini” — under Lochana's signature. Some of them are written in nagari-bhava, as if in the voice of the women of Nadia — a mood that the Gaudiya Vaishnavas, following Vrindavana Dasa, do not accept (see below); one pada under his name is in fact a passage from the “Chaitanya-mangala” itself, another belongs to Vasu Ghosha, and the playful conversational songs are usually linked with his “Dhamali” — dhamali songs about Gaura. Many of these padas are ascribed to him only by later collections, and so we speak of them as songs circulating under his name; Srila Bhaktisiddhanta expressly warns about the collections called “Lochana's panchali” (see below). Already N. Vasu (1897) held that the “Baramasya of Vishnupriya” bearing Lochana's signature was not composed by him.

Gaura Is Not a “Nagara”

One of the deviant communities (apasampradayas) claims that the “Chaitanya-mangala” contains the Gaura-nagari doctrine — of Gaura as a nagara, the lover of the women of Nadia. This is not true. Vrindavana Dasa already spoke against such worship:

“Therefore all the great souls never praise Gauranga with such a hymn as ‘Gauranga-nagara.’” (CB, Adi 15.30)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains in the “Gaudiya-bhashya”: Sri Gaurasundara is Krishna who has accepted the mood and radiance of Radha. Therefore, never abandoning the heart's mood of Radhika and the gopis — those who love (ashraya) — the mood of service to Sri Krishna, He did not act, as Krishna Himself does, in the role of the One toward whom love is directed (vishaya), and never displayed the ways of a “nagara” who looks at others' wives with the pride of an enjoyer. And though Gaurasundara is Vrajendranandana Himself, the Supreme Lord, to call Him a “nagara” is not permissible: it is contrary to the very spirit of service to Gaura-Krishna. Vrajendranandana is called Gopijana-vallabha, the Beloved of the gopis, but in Gaura's pastimes Krishna abides in the mood of separation (vipralambha).

Where, then, do the lines of the “Chaitanya-mangala” that are read in the Gaura-nagari spirit come from? One of the biographies answers: self-interested people inserted this doctrine and various invented descriptions contrary to siddhanta into the book — as even some secular scholars admit; there are no such insertions in the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” and the “Chaitanya-charitamrita,” and whatever disagrees with them the followers of Gaura do not accept as a conclusion.

And Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, in his preface to the poem, says: seeing the grace of its language and Lochana's heartfelt love for Gaura, some claim that he strays somewhat from the truth of pure bhakti. “We are not prepared to say so,” he writes, “for ‘the actions and gestures of a Vaishnava are not understood even by the wise.’11 May the abominable desire to impute the stench of the Gaura-nagari doctrine to Sri Chaitanya-mangala never take hold of our hearts.” The collections of popular songs that circulate under the name “Lochana's panchali,” he says, must be approached with special caution: into many of them the newfangled Gaura-nagari doctrine has been introduced. Thus the acharya guards both Lochana's honour and the purity of siddhanta: in the poem Gaura is Krishna in the mood and radiance of Radha, and to glorify Him as a “nagara” goes against the truth proclaimed by Vrindavana Dasa and Kaviraja Gosvami.

Departure and Samadhi

Lochana Dasa left this world, according to the biographies, in 1589.12 By our calendar (Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math) the day of his departure is Krishna-ashtami of the month of Madhava (≈ Magha); in 2027 it falls on 30 January. The biographies do not name this day. His brick samadhi stands at his shripat, over the resting place of his holy body; and Lochana's shripat is his native village, Kogram.

Significance

By his guru's will and with love for Gaura, Lochana Dasa became the singer of the Lord's pastimes for the simple people of Rarh: his panchalis are sung to this day, and through them Mahaprabhu's pastimes reach those who do not read Sanskrit poems. His life is a lesson in fidelity to the guru: everything he composed he held to be the mercy of Narahari and the Vaishnavas. His songs about Nityananda are a lesson in humility: even a shadow of inattention to Nityananda's glory Narahari's disciple took as a fault and made it good with songs that Vaishnavas sing to this day. And the way Srila Bhaktisiddhanta defended his poem against the Gaura-nagari doctrine imputed to it teaches us to read it with a Vaishnava's eyes: Gaura is Krishna in the mood of Radha, and the measure of every account of Him is the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” and the “Chaitanya-charitamrita.”

Notes

  1. He should not be confused with Sulochana of Shrikhanda, a branch of the tree of Sri Chaitanya (CC, Adi 10.78; Madhya 11.92; “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 209): Sulochana was with the Lord and came to Puri for the Ratha-yatra, whereas Lochana Dasa was born in 1523 and never saw the Lord. In the “Namamrita-samudra” of Narahari Chakravarti they are named separately: Thakura Lochana in v. 69, Sulochana in v. 75. Nor should his guru, Narahari Sarakara, be confused with Narahari Chakravarti (Ghanashyama Dasa), the author of the “Bhakti-ratnakara.”
  2. One of the biographies calls the place “Mahakumara” — a corruption of the word mahakuma (subdivision), not the name of a village. “Ten miles” and “five kroshas” are the same distance: a krosha is about two miles.
  3. One of the biographies calls his family brahmanas. We follow Lochana's own words (Shesha-khanda, 94+59), Srila Bhaktisiddhanta and the “Prema-vilasa” (19.413): he was a vaidya.
  4. Lochana's closing word about himself (Shesha-khanda, 94+39–94+69) is found only in the 1983 edition; it is absent from Srila Bhaktisiddhanta's edition (1922), and in the 1903 edition it is given in a footnote. Numbers such as “94+59” denote couplets added in the 1983 edition after v. 94 of Bhaktisiddhanta's edition.
  5. Close by, in 19.124, the “Prema-vilasa” names “Raghunandana and Sulochana,” and in 19.126 “Lochana”; that this is Lochana Dasa is very likely, but not beyond doubt.
  6. One of the biographies writes that Damodara Pandita, having heard Murari's verses, taught them to Lochana, who learned them by heart, that it was from Damodara too that Lochana heard the story from the “Jaimini-bharata,” and also that, according to Lochana, Murari's book is no longer in circulation, and so he conveys its essence in Bengali verse. Lochana himself says only that Damodara questioned Murari, and that he, Lochana, “heard” the finished book (Sutra-khanda 53–56); in the poem the story from the “Jaimini-bharata” is told by Murari in answer to Damodara's question; Damodara and Lochana could hardly have met in time. We follow Lochana's own words.
  7. According to some biographies the poem was completed in 1537, but Lochana would then have been only fourteen; it is usually assigned to the middle of the sixteenth century (the 1550s–1560s). N. Vasu, who in 1897–1898 published Jayananda's “Chaitanya-mangala,” held that Lochana's poem was composed long after the Lord's disappearance and after Jayananda's book — which is why Jayananda does not mention Lochana. On the tradition that Lochana's poem is older than the “Chaitanya-bhagavata,” see below.
  8. One of the biographies counts twelve chapters in the Madhya-khanda. The 1983 edition divides the text differently and adds a fourth chapter of the Shesha-khanda — on the Lord's disappearance — and Lochana's closing word about himself; they are absent from Bhaktisiddhanta's edition. In that chapter Lochana writes that the Lord “entered” (literally, “merged into”) Jagannatha. In the understanding of the Gaudiya Vaishnavas (Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati), the Lord's departure is His antardhana-lila: He only withdrew from worldly eyes, just as He appeared by His own will; His body is sat-chit-ananda, and there is no death for Him.
  9. Thus Lochana places the Lord's meeting with Ramananda Raya at Kanchi, whereas according to the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” (Madhya 8) it took place on the bank of the Godavari.
  10. The tradition that Lochana's poem is older than Vrindavana's book is hard to reconcile with the “Chaitanya-mangala” itself: already at its beginning (Sutra-khanda 35) Vrindavana's book is called the “Bhagavata.” N. Vasu (1897–1898) concluded from this very line that Lochana wrote after Vrindavana Dasa. We give it as a tradition.
  11. CC, Madhya 23.35 (in other editions 23.39): “Even the wise cannot understand the words, actions and ways of one in whose heart love for Krishna has risen.”
  12. Different years are given: 1589 (1511 of the Shaka era) according to some biographies; 1530 Shaka (1608) according to the “Vishvakosha,” to which one of them refers; “1540” according to another, with no era stated (1540 CE is impossible: Lochana would have been seventeen, and he wrote the poem later; if it is a Shaka year, it is 1618). The year of his appearance, 1523, is the same in all.
